items.label: Computation – Formal Decidability ≠ Human Judgment
items.notes: Algorithmic decidability concerns well-defined formal tasks.

items.label: Almost Everywhere
items.notes: A property holds almost everywhere if the set of exceptions has measure zero.

items.label: Automation ≠ Neutrality
items.notes: Automation replaces manual processes with algorithmic ones.

items.label: Banach–Tarski Theorem
items.notes: The Banach–Tarski theorem shows that, assuming the axiom of choice, a solid sphere can be decomposed and reassembled into two spheres of the same size.

items.label: Behavior ≠ Mental State
items.notes: Behavior is observable action.

items.label: Bell’s Theorem
items.notes: Bell’s theorem shows that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce all quantum predictions.

items.label: Beth Definability Theorem
items.notes: Beth’s theorem states that if a relation is implicitly definable in a theory (fixed by all models of the theory), then it is explicitly definable in the theory.

items.label: Busy Beaver Function
items.notes: The Busy Beaver function grows faster than any computable function.

items.label: Church–Turing Thesis
items.notes: It is often treated as a necessary truth about minds, nature, or physical reality.

items.label: Compactness Theorem
items.notes: The compactness theorem states that if every finite subset of a first-order theory is satisfiable, then the entire theory is satisfiable.

items.label: Consensus ≠ Evidence
items.notes: Consensus reflects social convergence.

items.label: Continuity ≠ Identity
items.notes: Continuity describes persistence over time.

items.label: Continuum Hypothesis
items.notes: The continuum hypothesis is independent of standard ZFC set theory.

items.label: Control ≠ Understanding
items.notes: Control enables prediction or manipulation.

items.label: Craig’s Interpolation Theorem
items.notes: If a sentence A entails a sentence B in first-order logic, then there exists an interpolant C using only the vocabulary shared by A and B such that A entails C and C entails B.

items.label: Definition ≠ Essence
items.notes: Definitions clarify usage within a framework.

items.label: Descartes – Cogito and Certainty
items.notes: The Cogito establishes minimal certainty within methodical doubt: doubting presupposes thinking.

items.label: Diagonal Lemma
items.notes: The diagonal lemma guarantees, for any sufficiently expressive formal system, the existence of sentences that refer to their own provability or unprovability.

items.label: Economics – Model Rationality ≠ Human Rationality
items.notes: Economic models use idealized rational agents.

items.label: Equivalence of Categories
items.notes: Two categories are equivalent if there exist functors between them that preserve all categorical structure up to natural isomorphism.

items.label: Meta – Explanation ≠ Ontology
items.notes: Explanatory success does not automatically entail ontological commitment.

items.label: Forcing
items.notes: Forcing constructs model extensions in which certain statements hold or fail.

items.label: Meta – Formal Necessity ≠ Metaphysical Necessity
items.notes: Formal necessity concerns derivability within a system.

items.label: Gödel’s Completeness Theorem
items.notes:
Gödel’s completeness theorem states that every logically valid formula of first-order logic is provable within a sound and complete proof system. Equivalently, if a sentence is true in all models of a first-order theory, then it is derivable from the axioms of that theory.

This result concerns the alignment of syntax and semantics *within first-order logic*. It does not address the expressive adequacy of first-order languages, nor does it claim that all mathematically meaningful truths are capturable in first-order form.

items.label: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems
items.notes: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems establish that any consistent, effectively axiomatized formal system strong enough to represent elementary arithmetic contains sentences that are not provable within that system. The result is purely proof-theoretic: it concerns what can and cannot be derived from axioms by formal rules.

items.label: Gödel – Incompleteness as Metaphysics (Fallacy)
items.notes: Gödel shows limits of formal systems regarding provability.

items.label: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
items.notes: The uncertainty principle sets lower bounds on simultaneous operator variances in quantum mechanics.

items.label: Hume – The Problem of Induction
items.notes: Hume exposes the difficulty of non-circularly justifying inductive inference.

items.label: Is ≠ Ought
items.notes: Descriptive statements report facts.

items.label: Kant – Categories as Conditions of Knowledge
items.notes: Kant’s categories (e.g., causality, substance) describe conditions for the possibility of experience and judgment, not properties of things-in-themselves.

items.label: Kolmogorov Complexity
items.notes: Kolmogorov complexity measures the length of the shortest description of an object.

items.label: Law – Validity ≠ Moral Truth
items.notes: Legal norms derive validity from institutional procedures.

items.label: Law of Large Numbers
items.notes: The law of large numbers states that, under suitable conditions, sample averages converge to expected values as the number of trials increases.

items.label: Meta – Limits of Knowledge ≠ Limits of Being
items.notes: Epistemic limits describe what can be known or proven.

items.label: Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem
items.notes: The Löwenheim–Skolem theorem states that if a first-order theory has an infinite model, then it has a countable model. This is a model-theoretic result about the expressive limits of first-order logic.

items.label: Meaning ≠ Reference
items.notes: Meaning concerns sense, use, or inferential role; reference concerns what a term picks out.

items.label: Modal Logic – Formal vs. Metaphysical Possibility
items.notes: Modal logic models necessity and possibility within formal semantics.

items.label: Cosmology – Multiverse: Heuristic ≠ Ontological Commitment
items.notes: Multiverse ideas arise in certain theoretical frameworks.

items.label: AI – Output Equivalence ≠ Understanding
items.notes: Models can replicate behavior without clear evidence of understanding.

items.label: Non-measurable Sets
items.notes: Assuming the axiom of choice, there exist sets that cannot be assigned a Lebesgue measure.

items.label: Operationalization ≠ Definition
items.notes: Operationalization specifies how a concept is measured.

items.label: Optimization ≠ Value
items.notes: Optimization maximizes a defined objective function.

items.label: Categoricity of Second-Order Arithmetic
items.notes: Second-order Peano arithmetic is categorical under full second-order semantics.

items.label: P vs NP Problem
items.notes: It is often claimed that a separation would prove human creativity non-algorithmic.

items.label: Paradoxes – Linguistic Pathology ≠ World Contradiction
items.notes: Paradoxes reveal tensions in language or axioms.

items.label: Plato – Forms and Reification
items.notes: The theory of Forms explains stability and generality of concepts.

items.label: Preference ≠ Welfare
items.notes: Preferences express choices or rankings.

items.label: Recht – Geltung ≠ moralische Wahrheit
items.notes: Rechtsnormen gelten aufgrund institutioneller Setzung, Verfahren, Anerkennung und Durchsetzbarkeit.

items.label: Reflection Principles
items.notes: Reflection principles allow certain meta-theoretic facts to be internalized incrementally.

items.label: Relative Consistency and Conservativity
items.notes: Relative consistency results show that if one theory is consistent, then another is consistent; conservativity results show that an extension does not prove new theorems of a certain kind in the base language.

items.label: Relativität – Rahmenabhängigkeit ≠ Irrealität von Zeit
items.notes: Relativitätstheorie zeigt, dass Zeitmessungen von Bezugssystemen abhängen (Zeitdilatation, Gleichzeitigkeit).

items.label: Relativity – Frame Dependence ≠ Nonexistence of Time
items.notes: Relativity shows time measurements depend on reference frames.

items.label: Reproducibility ≠ Truth
items.notes: Reproducibility shows stability under repetition.

items.label: Rice’s Theorem
items.notes: Rice’s theorem states that every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable.

items.label: Scalability ≠ Generality
items.notes: Scalability refers to performance growth with resources.

items.label: Second-Order Semantics: Full vs. Henkin
items.notes: Full semantics is treated as the uniquely correct or “intended” meaning of second-order logic, and Henkin semantics as a mere technical compromise.

items.label: Self-Model ≠ Self
items.notes: Self-models are representations within cognitive systems.

items.label: Set Theory – Mathematical vs. Real Existence
items.notes: In mathematics, existence typically means derivability within axioms or model-consistency.

items.label: Simulation – Simulierbarkeit ≠ Ersetzbarkeit/Identität
items.notes: Eine Simulation bildet ausgewählte Strukturen/Relationen eines Systems ab, oft mit idealisierten Annahmen.

items.label: Simulation – Simulatability ≠ Identity
items.notes: A simulation represents structural aspects of a system.

items.label: Soundness Theorem (First-Order Logic)
items.notes: A proof system is sound if every sentence provable in the system is valid in all models (i.e., derivability implies semantic consequence).

items.label: Statistical Significance ≠ Practical Relevance
items.notes: Statistical significance measures likelihood under a null model.

items.label: Statistics – Correlation ≠ Causation
items.notes: Correlation measures statistical association.

items.label: Statistik – Korrelation ≠ Kausalität
items.notes: Korrelation misst statistische Abhängigkeit; Kausalität verlangt ein Modell von Interventionen, Mechanismen oder Zeitrichtung.

items.label: Meta – Successful Model ≠ True Description
items.notes: Models can be highly predictive while idealized.

items.label: Symbol Manipulation ≠ Semantics
items.notes: Formal systems manipulate symbols according to syntactic rules.

items.label: Tarski’s Undefinability of Truth
items.notes: Tarski proved that for any sufficiently expressive formal language, a truth predicate for that language cannot be defined within the language itself.

items.label: Turing’s Halting Theorem
items.notes: Turing’s halting theorem proves that there is no general algorithm that can decide, for every program and input, whether the program halts. This is a result about computability, not about knowledge in general.

items.label: Quantum Theory – Wave Function: Representation ≠ Thing
items.notes: The wave function is a mathematical object used for prediction.

items.label: Wittgenstein – Language Games and Relativism
items.notes: Language games analyze meaning as use within practices.

items.label: Wittgenstein – Sprachspiele und Relativismus
items.notes: Sprachspiele und Lebensformen analysieren, wie Bedeutung durch Gebrauch und Praxis stabilisiert wird.

items.label: Yoneda Lemma
items.notes: The Yoneda lemma characterizes objects by their relations to all other objects in a category.

items.label: The method is exempt from its limits
The model does not apply to itself
The system cannot affect its own analysis
The tool does not shape outcomes
